'''Daniel Simberloff''' is an American [[biologist]] and [[ecologist]]. He earned his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1969.<ref name = Homepage>{{Cite web|url=https://eeb.utk.edu/people/daniel-simberloff/|title=Daniel Simberloff &#124; Ecology & Evolutionary Biology|accessdate=23 June 2023}}</ref> He is currently Gore Hunger Professor of Environmental Science at the [[University of Tennessee]],<ref name = Homepage />  editor-in-chief of the journal ''[[Biological Invasions (journal)|Biological Invasions]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.springer.com/journal/10530|title=Biological Invasions|website=Springer|accessdate=23 June 2023}}</ref> and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] of the USA.

==Early life and education== 
Simberloff received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[Harvard College]] in 1964, and his Ph.D. in biology from [[Harvard University]] in 1969.<ref name = Homepage /> He wanted to go to graduate school for [[mathematics]], but changed his mind after taking a major biology course from future Nobel Prize winner, [[George Wald]].<ref>Dritschilo, W. (2019). ''Earth Days Reprised''</ref>

== Career ==
Simberloff was a faculty member at [[Florida State University]] from 1968-1997 before relocating to the [[University of Tennessee]], [[Knoxville, Tennessee|Knoxville]]. He is currently a distinguished professor there in the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology.  His more recent work focuses on the presence of invasive species, and raises the "specter of 'invasional meltdown'". At present, Simberloff has a long-term project in [[Patagonia]] on the invasion of [[conifer]] trees, involving introduced [[deer]], [[Wild boar|boar]], and [[Fungus|fungi.]] Simberloff has a total of over 350 publications, and he is currently working on several papers on invasive biology.{{Citation needed|reason=Reliable source needed for entire paragraph|date=September 2021}}

==Academic Work==
Simberloff's doctoral dissertation tested the theory of [[island biogeography]] proposed by [[Robert H. MacArthur]] and Edward O. Wilson,<ref>MacArthur, R.H., and E. O. Wilson. (1967). The Theory of Island Biogeography. Princeton University Press.</ref> resulting in a paper<ref name = "Simberloff">{{Cite journal |last1=Simberloff |first1=Daniel |author-link=Daniel Simberloff |last2=Wilson |first2=Edward O. |authorlink2=E. O. Wilson |title=Experimental Zoogeography of islands - colonization of empty islands |journal=[[Ecology (journal)|Ecology]] |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=278–296 |publisher=[[Ecological Society of America]] |date=March 1969 |url=http://www.clas.ufl.edu/users/mbinford/GEOXXXX_Biogeography/LiteratureForLinks/Simberloff_and_Wilson_1969_colonization_of_empty_islands_Ecology.pdf |doi=10.2307/1934856 |jstor=1934856 |accessdate=2010-09-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121215043322/http://www.clas.ufl.edu/users/mbinford/GEOXXXX_Biogeography/LiteratureForLinks/Simberloff_and_Wilson_1969_colonization_of_empty_islands_Ecology.pdf |archive-date=2012-12-15 |url-status=dead }}</ref> that won the [[Ecological Society of America]]'s Mercer Award in 1971<ref name="esa.org">{{Cite web|url=https://esa.org/history/mercer-award/#tablepress-3_wrapper|title = George Mercer Award – Historical Records Committee &#124; Ecological Society of America}}</ref> and was included as one of forty classic papers that represented the foundations of ecology.<ref>Real, L. A., and J. H. Brown.(1991). ''Foundations of Ecology: Classic Papers with Commentaries''. The University of Chicago Press.</ref> He began to be concerned that most mathematical models "more or less fit some data but had no reason to be the preferred explanation."<ref>Dritschilo, W. (2008). Bringing Statistical Methods to Community and Evolutionary Ecology: Daniel S. Simberloff. P. 360.</ref> He showed that a random draw could explain some patterns having to do with island [[Biota (biology)|biota]].<ref>Simberloff, D. S., (1970). Taxonomic Diversity of Island Biota. ''Evolution'' '''24''':23-47.</ref> Meanwhile, a number of biologists, such as [[Jared Diamond]], began calling for island biogeography theory to be applied in conservation.<ref>Diamond, J. M. (1975). The Island Dilemma: Lessons of Island Biogeography for the Design of Nature Reserves. ''Biological Conservation''. '''7''':129-146.</ref> This became a controversy in ecology known as the [[SLOSS debate]]. In his 1976 ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' paper, Simberloff contradicted his own theory, claiming that most of the insect turnover in the assemblages studied was [[Ephemerality|ephemeral]] and did not, therefore, confirm island biogeography theory in general. In fact, two smaller areas could mathematically support more species than a single area of the same size, and he had experimental data from his mangrove studies to support it.<ref>Simberloff, D. S., and L, G. Abele. (1976). ''Science'' '''191''':285-286.</ref> A leading proponent of the theory now writes that "the [[Species–area relationship|species-area curve]] is a blunt tool in many contexts" and "now seems simplistic to the point of being cartoonish" when it comes to management of nature preserves.<ref>Laurance, W. F. (2008). Theory Meets reality: How Habitat Fragmentation Research has Transcended Island Biogeographic Theory. ''Biological Conservation'' '''141''':1731-44.</ref>

Simberloff then took on the [[Robert MacArthur|MacArthurian]] paradigm of competitively structured communities, championing the use of null models in [[community ecology]].<ref>Gotelli, N. J., and R. G. Graves. (1996). ''Null Models in Ecology.'' Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D. C.</ref> Debate on the subject in the ecological literature became so heated that it inspired the name of "[[Tallahassee, Florida|Tallahassee]] mafia" for Simberloff and his associates at Florida State University.<ref>Lewin, R.  (1983). Santa Rosalia Was a Goat. ''Science'' '''221''':636-9.</ref> Its high points were a set of papers in a philosophical journal,<ref>Multiple authors. (1980). ''Synthese'' 43:3-93.</ref> an entire issue of ''[[The American Naturalist]]'',<ref>A Round Table on Research in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology. (1983). ''The American Naturalist'' '''122''':583-705.</ref> and a published symposium at [[Wakulla Springs|Wakulla Springs, Florida]],<ref>Strong, D. R., Jr., Simberloff, D., Abele, L. G., and A. B Thistle. (1984). Editors, ''Ecological Communities: Conceptual Issues and the Evidence''. Princeton University Press, Princeton, New Jersey, .</ref> that changed the face of the field.{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}} Simberloff caused ecologists to ask "what would happen if one mechanism were removed?" He preached, "rely on the data to tell you how nature operates; don't simply find the patterns that you're supposed to find." The [[Ecological Society of America]] conferred on him its 2006 Eminent Ecologist Award for his "outstanding body of ecological work" and "contributions of extraordinary merit," citing him in particular for having been "the quintessential ecological [[Iconoclasm|iconoclast]]."<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite web|url=https://www.esa.org/history/Awards/bulletin/eminent2006.pdf|title=Eminent Ecologist Award Daniel Simberloff|website=esa.org|access-date=23 June 2023}}</ref>

== Other professional work ==
Simberloff was instrumental in the promulgation of presidential [[Executive Order]] 13112 on invasive species, and also serves on the IUCN Invasive Species Specialist Group and the [[IUCN Species Survival Commission]]. He has served on the Board of Governors of the [[The Nature Conservancy|Nature Conservancy]], the federal [[Invasive Species Advisory Committee]], and the editorial boards of ''Biodiversity and Conservation'', ''Oecologia'', ''Biological Invasions'', ''BioScience'' and ''Ecology''.

* 2012: Elected to [[The National Academy of Sciences]]
* 2012: Elected Fellow of the Ecological Society of America<ref>{{Cite web |title=ESA Fellows |url=https://esa.org/about/awards/fellows-program/esa-fellows/ |access-date=2025-08-13 |website=Ecological Society of America}}</ref>
